notes.definition: If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic in the opposite direction. The same amount of energy is transferred in each case.
explanation: Every chemical reaction involves an energy change with the surroundings. An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises. An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls (or the reaction needs to be heated to keep going).

In a reversible reaction, the forward and reverse reactions have opposite energy changes. If the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction must be endothermic, and if the forward reaction is endothermic, the reverse reaction must be exothermic. The amount of energy transferred is exactly the same in each direction. For example, if the forward reaction takes in 78 kJ, the reverse reaction for the same amount of substance gives out 78 kJ. Energy is conserved, so you cannot get more or less energy back by reversing the reaction.

The classic example is copper sulfate. Hydrated copper sulfate is blue because it contains water in its crystals. When it is heated, the water is driven off and white anhydrous copper sulfate is left. This forward reaction is endothermic, because energy must be supplied by heating. When water is added to the white anhydrous copper sulfate, it turns blue again and becomes hot. This reverse reaction is exothermic.
hydrated copper sulfate (blue) ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate (white) + water
endothermic forwards, exothermic backwards

The colour change from white to blue is used as a test for water: if a liquid turns white anhydrous copper sulfate blue, the liquid contains water. This test shows that water is present but does not show that the water is pure. The thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride is another example: it is endothermic when ammonium chloride is heated and splits up, and exothermic when ammonia and hydrogen chloride react to reform the solid.

On an energy level diagram, the reactants and products of a reversible reaction are drawn at two different energy levels. The forward and reverse reactions move between the same two levels in opposite directions, so the energy change has the same size but the opposite sign. An energy change written as +X kJ (energy taken in) for the forward reaction becomes −X kJ (energy given out) for the reverse reaction.
keyFacts: If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic in the opposite direction.
The same amount of energy is transferred in each direction.
Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings, so the temperature rises.
Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature falls.
hydrated copper sulfate (blue) ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate (white) + water
Heating hydrated copper sulfate is endothermic.
Adding water to anhydrous copper sulfate is exothermic: it turns blue and gets hot.
White anhydrous copper sulfate turning blue is a test for water.
Decomposing ammonium chloride is endothermic; reforming it is exothermic.
If the forward energy change is +X kJ, the reverse energy change is −X kJ.

keyTerms.definition: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Blue copper sulfate crystals that contain water (water of crystallisation).
White copper sulfate that contains no water; it turns blue when water is added.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, so the energy taken in by one direction of a reversible reaction equals the energy given out by the other.
A diagram showing the relative energies of the reactants and products, and whether energy is taken in or given out.

workedExamples.title: Energy change of the reverse reaction
workedExamples.question: In the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). The forward reaction gives out 92 kJ when 2 moles of ammonia are formed. How much energy is transferred when 2 moles of ammonia decompose into nitrogen and hydrogen? Is this exothermic or endothermic?
steps: The forward reaction is exothermic (energy given out).
The reverse reaction must therefore be endothermic.
The same amount of energy is transferred in each direction, so the reverse reaction takes in 92 kJ.
workedExamples.answer: 92 kJ is taken in; the reverse reaction is endothermic.

workedExamples.title: Scaling the energy change
workedExamples.question: Heating 1 mole of hydrated copper sulfate to form anhydrous copper sulfate takes in 78 kJ. How much energy is given out when water is added to 0.25 moles of anhydrous copper sulfate to reform the hydrated salt?
steps: The reverse reaction (adding water) is exothermic and transfers the same amount of energy per mole: 78 kJ per mole.

workedExamples.title: Reading an energy level diagram
workedExamples.question: On an energy level diagram, the reactants of a reversible reaction are at 40 kJ and the products are at 105 kJ. Find the energy change for the forward and reverse reactions.
steps: Forward energy change = products − reactants = 105 − 40 = +65 kJ, so the forward reaction is endothermic.
The reverse reaction goes from 105 kJ back down to 40 kJ: 40 − 105 = −65 kJ.
The reverse reaction is exothermic, with the same size of energy change.
workedExamples.answer: Forward +65 kJ (endothermic); reverse −65 kJ (exothermic, 65 kJ given out).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that both directions of a reversible reaction can be exothermic.
misconceptions.right: In fact if one direction is exothermic, the other must be endothermic.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the reverse reaction transfers less energy than the forward reaction because some is 'used up'.
misconceptions.right: In fact exactly the same amount of energy is transferred in each direction; only the direction of transfer changes.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that anhydrous copper sulfate turning blue proves a liquid is pure water.
misconceptions.right: In fact it only shows that water is present. A pure substance test (such as boiling point) is needed to show the water is pure.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that heating hydrated copper sulfate is exothermic because it gets hot.
misconceptions.right: In fact the solid gets hot because it is being heated. The reaction takes in energy from the flame, so it is endothermic.

realWorld: Anhydrous copper sulfate (or test papers containing it) is used to detect water, for example in fuels or in products of combustion.
Some reusable hand warmers and heat storage systems use reversible reactions or processes: energy is stored by driving the endothermic direction and released later by the exothermic direction.
In the Haber process the forward reaction making ammonia is exothermic, so the reverse reaction (ammonia breaking down) is endothermic; engineers must remove the heat released.
examTips: If you are told the energy change for one direction, the other direction has the same number with the opposite sign: just swap exothermic and endothermic.
Learn the copper sulfate colours: hydrated is blue, anhydrous is white. Do not say 'clear' or 'colourless' for anhydrous copper sulfate.
When describing the test for water, give both the starting colour and the final colour: white to blue.
Check whether a question asks for energy 'taken in' or 'given out' and use the correct words; a negative sign means energy is given out.
summary: Reversible reactions are exothermic in one direction and endothermic in the other.
The same amount of energy is transferred in each direction.
Heating blue hydrated copper sulfate (endothermic) gives white anhydrous copper sulfate and water.
Adding water to anhydrous copper sulfate is exothermic: it turns blue and gets hot.
White to blue anhydrous copper sulfate is a test for water.
If forward is +X kJ, reverse is −X kJ.

questions.question: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. What type of reaction is the reverse reaction?
markScheme: 1 mark: endothermic
questions.explanation: If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic in the opposite direction.

questions.question: What colour is anhydrous copper sulfate?
markScheme: 1 mark: white
questions.explanation: Anhydrous copper sulfate contains no water and is a white powder. Hydrated copper sulfate is blue. It is a solid, so 'colourless' is wrong.

questions.question: Water is added to white anhydrous copper sulfate. What is observed?
markScheme: 1 mark: it turns blue and gets hot
questions.explanation: Hydrated copper sulfate (blue) reforms. This direction of the reaction is exothermic, so energy is given out and the mixture gets hot.
options: It turns black and cools down
It stays white and gets hot
It turns blue and gets hot
It turns blue and gets colder

questions.question: Which word describes the reaction when water is added to anhydrous copper sulfate?
markScheme: 1 mark: exothermic
questions.explanation: Energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature rises. The reverse direction, heating the blue crystals, is endothermic.

questions.question: A reversible reaction takes in 50 kJ in the forward direction. What happens in the reverse direction for the same amount of substance?
markScheme: 1 mark: 50 kJ is given out
questions.explanation: The reverse reaction is exothermic and transfers exactly the same amount of energy, 50 kJ, but to the surroundings.

questions.question: White anhydrous copper sulfate is used in a chemical test. What does the test show?
markScheme: 1 mark: whether water is present
questions.explanation: It turns blue when water is present. It does not show whether the water is pure; other substances could be dissolved in it.
options: Whether a gas is carbon dioxide
Whether a liquid is pure water

questions.question:
Ammonium chloride decomposes when heated: ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride
The forward reaction is endothermic. Which statement describes the reaction when ammonia and hydrogen chloride react?
markScheme: 1 mark: exothermic, same amount of energy
questions.explanation: The reverse of an endothermic reaction is exothermic, and the energy transferred is equal in size.
options: It is exothermic and transfers the same amount of energy as the forward reaction
It is endothermic and transfers the same amount of energy
It is exothermic and transfers less energy than the forward reaction
It is endothermic and transfers more energy

questions.question:
Nitrogen dioxide forms dinitrogen tetroxide: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g)
The forward reaction gives out 57 kJ for the amounts in the equation. Which describes the decomposition of 1 mole of N₂O₄ into 2 moles of NO₂?
markScheme: 1 mark: 57 kJ taken in
questions.explanation: Decomposing 1 mole of N₂O₄ into 2 moles of NO₂ is exactly the reverse of the equation as written, so it is endothermic and takes in the same 57 kJ. Halving or doubling would only be needed if the amounts were different from the equation.

questions.question: A student adds a few drops of a colourless liquid to white anhydrous copper sulfate. It turns blue. What can the student conclude?
markScheme: 1 mark: the liquid contains water
questions.explanation: The test only shows that water is present. The liquid could be a solution containing water, for example salt water, so it cannot show purity.

questions.question:
A reversible reaction transfers 120 kJ to the surroundings in the forward direction.
Determine the energy taken in by the reverse reaction, for the same amounts.
markScheme: 1 mark: 120 kJ
questions.explanation: The same amount of energy is transferred in each direction. The forward reaction gives out 120 kJ, so the reverse reaction takes in 120 kJ.

questions.question:
Heating 1 mole of hydrated copper sulfate to form anhydrous copper sulfate and water takes in 78 kJ.
Calculate the energy given out when water is added to 0.25 moles of anhydrous copper sulfate.
markScheme: 1 mark: reverse reaction gives out 78 kJ per mole
questions.explanation: The reverse reaction is exothermic and transfers 78 kJ per mole. For 0.25 moles: 0.25 × 78 = 19.5 kJ.

questions.question:
A student added water to anhydrous copper sulfate in a polystyrene cup.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the temperature change.
markScheme: 1 mark: 11.5 °C
questions.explanation: Temperature change = final − initial = 31.0 − 19.5 = 11.5 °C. The temperature rises because this direction of the reaction is exothermic.

questions.question:
In the Haber process: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
Forming 2 moles of ammonia gives out 92 kJ.
Calculate the energy taken in when 5 moles of ammonia decompose into nitrogen and hydrogen.
markScheme: 1 mark: 46 kJ taken in per mole of NH₃ (92 ÷ 2)
questions.explanation: The reverse reaction is endothermic. 92 kJ for 2 moles is 46 kJ per mole, so 5 moles take in 5 × 46 = 230 kJ. Check: 92 × 2.5 = 230 kJ.

questions.question:
A reversible reaction has a forward energy change of +40 kJ.
State the energy change of the reverse reaction and explain your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: −40 kJ (40 kJ given out / exothermic)
1 mark: the same amount of energy is transferred in each direction (energy is conserved)
questions.explanation: The forward reaction takes in 40 kJ. The reverse reaction must give out the same 40 kJ, so its energy change is −40 kJ.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a student heating hydrated copper sulfate.
The student says: 'The hydrated copper sulfate gets hot, so the reaction must be exothermic.'
Explain why the student is wrong.

markScheme: 1 mark: the solid is hot because energy is being supplied by heating
1 mark: the reaction takes in energy (from the flame), so it is endothermic
questions.explanation: A reaction is endothermic if it takes in energy. The temperature of the solid rises because the flame supplies energy, and some of this energy is used by the reaction.
acceptedAnswers: the heat comes from the Bunsen burner
energy is taken in from the flame

questions.question: Describe the energy level diagram for a reversible reaction in which the forward reaction is exothermic. In your answer, state the positions of the reactants and products, and compare the arrows for the forward and reverse reactions.
markScheme: 1 mark: products drawn at a lower energy than reactants
1 mark: forward arrow points down (energy given out) and reverse arrow points up (energy taken in)
1 mark: both arrows are the same length / same size of energy change
questions.explanation: In an exothermic forward reaction the products are lower in energy. The reverse reaction goes between the same two levels in the opposite direction.

questions.question: Describe an experiment to show that the copper sulfate reaction is reversible and to show the energy changes in each direction. Include your observations.
markScheme: Indicative content: place blue hydrated copper sulfate in a boiling tube or evaporating basin; heat it with a Bunsen burner; observe it turning white as water is driven off (steam or condensation seen); this direction needs heating, so it is endothermic; allow the white anhydrous copper sulfate to cool; add a few drops of water; observe it turning blue again; measure the temperature with a thermometer or feel the tube: it gets hot; this direction is exothermic; the same reaction goes in both directions, so it is reversible; wear eye protection, as hot solid may spit.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear method covering both directions with colour changes and correct energy changes linked to observations.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes one direction or gives colour changes without energy changes.
questions.explanation: Make sure you describe both directions, with the colour change and the energy change for each.

questions.question:
Heating 1 mole of hydrated copper sulfate takes in 78 kJ.
A student added water to anhydrous copper sulfate in a glass beaker. The student used the temperature rise to work out the energy given out.
Table 1 shows the results.
Suggest and explain reasons why the student's value is lower than the expected value.

rows: Energy taken in when hydrated copper sulfate is heated
Energy given out when water is added to anhydrous copper sulfate (student's value)

markScheme: Indicative content: the true value for the reverse reaction should be 78 kJ per mole because the same amount of energy is transferred in each direction; energy is lost to the surroundings (air, beaker), so the measured temperature rise is too small; a glass beaker conducts heat; use a polystyrene cup with a lid to reduce losses; the anhydrous copper sulfate may not have been fully anhydrous (some water already absorbed from the air), so less reaction took place; not all of the anhydrous copper sulfate may have reacted with the water; the thermometer may not have been read at the maximum temperature.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): states the expected value of 78 kJ with reason, and explains at least two sensible sources of the lower value.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): gives one reason, such as heat loss, with limited explanation.
questions.explanation: The theory says the energy given out should equal the energy taken in. Practical values are usually lower because energy escapes to the surroundings.

questions.question:
Hydrated copper sulfate takes part in a reversible reaction.
Explain the colour changes and energy changes that happen in this reversible reaction, and how this reaction is used as a chemical test. Include a word equation in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: hydrated copper sulfate (blue) ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate (white) + water; heating blue hydrated copper sulfate drives off water; it turns white; the forward reaction is endothermic because energy has to be supplied; adding water to white anhydrous copper sulfate turns it blue; this reverse reaction is exothermic, the mixture gets hot; if a reversible reaction is endothermic in one direction it is exothermic in the other; the same amount of energy is transferred in each direction; for example if 78 kJ is taken in per mole, 78 kJ is given out per mole; anhydrous copper sulfate is used to test for water; white to blue shows water is present; the test does not show whether water is pure.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct equation, both colour changes, both energy changes with the idea of equal amounts of energy, and the test for water explained.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes both colour changes and at least one correct energy change, with some reference to the test for water.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about colours or energy, with little linking.
questions.explanation: A full answer links each direction to its colour change and energy change, states that the energy amounts are equal, and explains the water test.
